The Hida salamander (Hynobius kimurae) is a stream-breeding hynobiid endemic to cool, forested mountain streams in central Japan. Hatchlings emerge from gelatinous egg sacs deposited in the stream at a snout-vent length at birth of 1.05 centimeters [Lb = 1.05 centimeters], with a corresponding wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0077 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0077 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of about 2.45 millimeters. At a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the age at birth reaches approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], reflecting the slow embryonic development characteristic of cold montane stream habitats.

Following hatching, the aquatic larva undergoes a period of growth before completing metamorphosis, attaining a snout-vent length at metamorphosis of 2.95 centimeters . The recently metamorphosed juvenile then transitions to a semi-terrestrial existence in the leaf litter and rocky crevices bordering the natal stream, returning to the water only for subsequent breeding. Growth continues over several years thereafter as the animal accumulates the somatic reserves necessary for reproductive maturity.

Sexual maturation in this species is notably delayed and differs between the sexes. At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females reaches approximately 7 years [tp = approximately 7 years], while males mature somewhat earlier, with a time since birth at puberty for males of approximately 5 years [tp = approximately 5 years]. This protracted juvenile period is consistent with the slow pace of life typical of cold-adapted, stream-dwelling salamanders, which must accumulate sufficient body condition before their first breeding migration.

Adults of Hynobius kimurae ultimately attain an ultimate SVL of 9.7 centimeters [Li = 9.7 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 7.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.6 grams], a value estimated from length-weight scaling relationships derived from the related Onychodactylus japonicus. Reproductive output is concentrated in a single annual clutch: at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females deposit their eggs in a pair of gelatinous sacs, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 51 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 51 eggs per year]. Longevity in this species reaches a maximum of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] at the same reference temperature, a considerable lifespan that, combined with delayed maturation and modest annual fecundity, reflects a slow, K-selected life-history strategy well suited to the stable, resource-limited headwater streams this salamander inhabits at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C].
